utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-04-75-T, the Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. For the Prosecution, Douglas Stringer, Sarah Clanton, case manager Thomas Laugel, legal intern Katherine Davis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zivanovic, for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Christopher Gosnell, with case manager Negosava Smiljanic, and intern Milan Jovancevic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Hadzic, yesterday we talked about that letter that was written by Marin Vidic, Bili, about -- well, I mean, you said something about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It's 1D762.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please tell us, this letter and the situation that Mr. Vidic wrote about in that letter, was that a well-known thing in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was a well-known thing. Practically everyone knew about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would tender this document, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D124, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me now whether you remember the incidents that occurred at that time, so we're already in the month of August, in general terms, things that happened in the area, in the region of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I remember most of these incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were any of your acquaintances or relatives or friends a direct casualty of the activities taken by the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I mentioned some names yesterday. There were quite a few of my acquaintances and good friends who were casualties, who were killed, both in Vukovar and in Borovo Naselje, and throughout this area. Except for Baranja. I didn't know anyone in Baranja at the time. So it's Slavonia and Western Srem. And the information I had from Baranja, well, I knew the names, but I did not know those people. I hadn't known them before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember the locations where these conflicts were taking place at the time, as well as these attacks of Croatian forces against Serb villages and Serbs?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the closest incident to me was Brsadin. That's the first one I remember. Simo Konjevic was killed there. I think that was before the 1st of August. It was in June or the end of June. There was this incident in Sarvas where several civilians were killed. I remember the Adamovic family. Maybe the largest numbers were in Vukovar itself and Borovo Naselje. And in Sotin, Mihajlo Nadj was killed there. He was a member of the Serb Democratic Party, but I think that one of his parents was a Hungarian and the other one was a Serb, but I'm not sure about that. I know some names from Vukovar too. I've already mentioned them. Jovan Jakovljevic, Mladen Mrkic, Tomo Jakovljevic and his wife. Vlado Skeledzija went missing and quite a few other people. Savo Damjanovic, who worked at the hospital, he was a friend of mine, he was killed. So Mladen Mrkic and Savo Damjanovic. I've just mentioned some names now. I don't want to go on because I don't really want to skip anyone so I've just -- I've just mentioned a couple.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see, please, 1D299.1. Sorry. 249. That's good. 241 -- 249.1. Yes. [Interpretation] This is a press release of the Permanent Mission of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the Permanent Mission of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to the UN. So could we please take a look at the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please take a look at Roman I-003.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Please take a look, and do you see that this incident involving Mihajlo Nadj is mentioned here?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you something: I see that the names of the perpetrators of these crime, or, rather, the suspects are mentioned here. Do you know whether any of them were held accountable for that? Were any proceedings instituted against them, against the perpetrators of this crime?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that. I don't know who the perpetrators are.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You also mentioned the crime in Sarvas. Could you please take a look at one -- Roman numeral I-005 and then 006 at the same time. It's the same place, it's the same date.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those are the crimes that I mentioned a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D125.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, yesterday I mentioned a friend of mine who had been killed and I said that his name was Slobodan. Out of respect for the deceased, I remembered his last name, Vuckovic; Slobodan Vuckovic. He was executed in Borovo Naselje. He was shot dead in front of a wall, just like in the Second World War. That's what I heard later from eye-witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when this happened, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That happened either towards the end of June or mid-July, so it was before the war. I've just remembered his last name now. I couldn't remember before.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who it was that executed him?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the information I had then, he was executed by the Croatian reserve police force, but I don't know the actual names. And when I said the "reserve police force," that should be taken relatively conditionally. I don't know this exactly, but at any rate, he was killed by the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You spoke to us about the situation with the refugees at the very beginning of this crisis. I would be interested in hearing what the situation concerning refugees was at that time, when these conflicts had become more widespread there, so the month of August. Do you remember? I'm talking about refugees from Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, the ones that found refuge in Serbia and Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, yesterday I had a conversation with the interpreters and about the problem -- problems with their work. One of the problems is your microphone that is open when the witness answers the questions, and while you're moving around your papers, there's a lot of background noise. So you should try to close your microphone as soon as Mr. Hadzic starts talking. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll do my best, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The number of refugees was proportionate to the increase in combat operations. So as combat operations increased, the number of refugees increased, to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see please 1D826. 826. [Microphone not activated]. 826.1, please -- 826.1. My microphone was not on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to ask you to take a look at this text that has to do with refugees. It is very short, and it says here that -- this is the 29th of August, 1991. And that 73.588 refugees were registered then. My question: This number, was it realistic? Were you aware of it at the time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, it was realistic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would tender this document, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D126, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, yesterday you spoke about the operation of taking or liberating Dalj - depends on your angle - in 1991. This is what I'm interested in: After that, did you move to Dalj? You said that until then you were in Borovo Selo. Before that, you didn't really have the right conditions for working. Did the moment come when you went to Dalj? Would you please describe that to us.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the beginning of August, maybe seven or six days after the 1st of August, I came to Dalj. And there, for the first time, I was given some offices, premises where I could stay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What kind of premises?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The locals continue to call that building Bozidar Maslaric house. That's what I knew it as later. I knew it as the town library. Those premises were not adequate but it was the only thing that I had at the time. Until then, I had absolutely nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was there anyone else there?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't seem to remember that anybody else used it as offices, but there were residents of Dalj who came and went. There were people there almost all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When was the first time you met Radovan Stojicic, Badza?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite soon after my move to Dalj, while I was on those large premises. It could have been perhaps on the third day after I moved there. Maybe the seventh day. But it was, in any case, in the first half of August. He came into that library. He was wearing a uniform and carried a Heckler with a silencer. That was the first time I saw a silencer. And he had some sort of black uniform with the lettering "police." Or maybe it was navy with some sort of insignia. But it was a combat uniform, a dark combat uniform, of the police. He introduced himself as Radovan Stojicic, Badza. He said: I am a high-ranking official of the MUP of Serbia, and I am here to take over the Territorial Defence. There were two other men with him in the same uniform, also armed with Hecklers, and I knew them by sight because they had earlier been checking on people crossing the Danube. I thought they were the highest ranking policemen in Serbia, and then I realised that Radovan Stojicic, Badza, was their boss, so they were unimportant. One was called Zavisic and the other Bogunovic. There was a fourth man, also carrying a Heckler with a silencer on it, but he was wearing a green camouflage uniform. It was not a military uniform. Badza said: This man is Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, and he will be the commander of special units. I don't remember if I said anything or if I said: Okay. And then I watched through the window as they got into their jeeps. Some of the jeeps had police licence plates, and one of them maybe had Belgrade licence plates. And I watched them drive away.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We did not hear the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They had the letter M, followed by a number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I repeat my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the record, you have already answered it. What did the police licence plates look like?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a letter M followed by a number, and they were blue. Some of the vehicles were also blue. They were of a make called Puch. And there were also Mitsubishi Pajero, also blue. I had not seen such vehicles in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem before, especially not so many of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, did Radovan Stojicic ask anything of you? Did he have any demands during your first meeting?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't ask for anything, and he didn't ask me any questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did he perhaps ask where they could find accommodation? There were quite a few of them.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, he asked me absolutely nothing, which means he didn't ask me about accommodation either. I thought it was their first day there. I thought they had just arrived. But when I heard the testimony of Witness 003, I realised they had arrived earlier. I think, at least, that it's 003; I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did Radovan Stojicic, Badza, ask of you or of the government of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem to be appointed commander of the Territorial Defence of the SBWS?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never. And that was never even discussed. To us, Badza was a representative of the federal state and that's the capacity in which he arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, counsel, I -- Mr. President, I was just noticing, I think that one of the names that Mr. Hadzic mentioned has been left out of the transcript at page 8, line 9. He said that there were two people arrived with Badza and only one of the names, I think, appears in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll repeat the question. Mr. Hadzic, would you repeat for the record the names of the people who arrived with Badza.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Badza was accompanied by two men wearing the same uniform as Badza and a third man wearing a slightly different uniform. All of them had the same weapon, namely, a Heckler with a silencer on it. The one in the different uniform was Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan; whereas the others wearing blue uniforms were Nebojsa Zavisic and Milorad Bogunovic. Miodrag Zavisic and Nebojsa Bogunovic. Zavisic is spelled Z-a-v-i-s-i-c.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Just one moment, Mr. Zivanovic. I take it ... no, it's already corrected. Sorry. Please continue, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you tell me, please, when did you learn where they found accommodation?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought they were in Erdut because I didn't know they had come earlier. I learned that from the witness. I heard then that they had been in the village but, in fact, after that, they went to the centre in Erdut. That's where they were staying. That's when I saw them. As far as Arkan is concerned, I heard he was in Tenja. The village of Tenja near Osijek.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In that period of June, July, August, did you go to Tenja?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't go to Tenja. And I even wasn't able to go; I didn't have a car.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When did you learn that Radovan Stojicic, Badza, and Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, and their men were accommodated in Erdut?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard from some friends of mine that later become members of the government, specifically, I think, Vojo Susa who was not from this part of Slavonia and Baranja that was under our control. His house had been left behind in Vinkovci and he had nowhere to sleep when he was in Slavonia and Baranja. He told me that there was a centre in Erdut that belonged either to the former TO of Croatia or the JNA where he spent nights. And I went to see that, and I found accommodation there for myself because I had nowhere to spend nights either. I wasn't able to go to Pacetin because I couldn't use a normal car. Only an all-terrain vehicle could use that road, so I either slept there or I would across the Danube and sleep in Serbia. I went there, and I met Dragomir Lastavica who had been the manager of that centre even before the war. This man, Dragomir Lastavica, introduced me to a lieutenant-colonel, and I can't remember whether the last name was Stosic or Raskovic. I realise the two are not similar but I can't remember. Witnesses mentioned different names and I can't recall myself. So they gave me a room upstairs where I could spend nights when I needed to. I spent nights there, maybe two or three times within those 15 or 20 days, and after that, Arkan and Badza showed up. My driver, Milenko Japundzic, told me that Arkan had beaten up that lieutenant-colonel and thrown him out, literally kicked him in the butt. I couldn't believe it. So I asked Dragomir Lastavica whether that was true, and he said yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that at some point in Erdut you saw Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, and Radovan Stojicic, Badza, with your own eyes?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw them with my own eyes. During the day, they were not there; at least not by the time I got up. They would be already gone, either into combat or for training. But when I came at night to spend the night there, I saw them sitting together, because the stairs that I used to go upstairs to my room overlooked that large mess room. I didn't spend nights there often, but I did see them once or twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how long you stayed in that building? How long did you use that room that you described? Was there a moment - and when - when you moved somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even when I was there, I did not sleep there often, perhaps once a week or maybe twice a week. But then I moved to a flat. I moved to a flat which was next to the building that was used by the government for its sessions. It was a manor building. And, yes, now I have just remembered that I need to explain something else. I learned about that manor from Slavko Dokmanovic because before all the others, he found accommodation there in the best of the rooms in the manor that used to belong to the CO of the winery. And then I was given an office as well, which you entered from the corridor. It could not just be a little room with a secretary, like Dokmanovic said, because that's how things were. I was happy with that because the conditions that I had to live in before were worse, and I even got a telephone line there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that before that you did not have a telephone line?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a telephone in the library in Dalj in a small room there, but it was just for local calls within Dalj and even that was erratic, as far as I can remember. Before we moved to Erdut, a telephone number was introduced with the 025 aerial code. That was for Sombor. But I never used it before we moved to Erdut. The secretary of the government used that telephone, the one who remained in Dalj.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand your last answer about your accommodation. Were you accommodated in the manor building or in the building next to the manor building?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a building 4 metres away from the manor building itself, a newer building that was built for the former IPK Osijek, which was an industrial and agricultural company of Osijek. It was built for their CEO. It was quite a nice building with very expensive furniture.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As you have just told us, apart from Slavko Dokmanovic and yourself, did any other government members find accommodation in Erdut?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, the entire government was in Erdut. However, in the main part of the manor building where Dokmanovic was, and that was the first room on the left-hand side as you enter the corridor, and the next room was a big room where the government sessions were held. And then straight on, along the corridor, was the room where I was. Next to my room or my office there was another office where Dr. Hadzic and Sabljakovic were accommodated. On the right-hand side was the toilet and there was also a restaurant in that main building. The outbuilding or, rather, the building that was an extension to the manor, there were a few more rooms where ministries were housed or, rather, two or three ministers shared an office. I never entered any of those rooms where the ministers were sitting, or perhaps just once. There was just one secretary there in the main building. She was Dokmanovic's secretary. I didn't have a secretary. I didn't have any members of staff. It was only when I became the president of the republic, after I arrived in Knin, that I was given my first secretary.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, when you say that the ministers had rooms there, did they use those rooms as offices or as their private accommodation?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, those were their offices. Nobody lived on the ground floor, although there was the circular staircase leading to the first floor but I don't know who slept there. I never climbed that staircase. The most important thing for us was the restaurant because when I was in Dalj, there was no place for me to eat. In Dalj, I ate in a soup kitchen for the poor. I had to have a meal a day at least, and there were no other public restaurants where you could go and eat.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know anything before you saw the four people who arrived in Dalj? Did you know anything about Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan; and, if you did, what did you know?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew two things perhaps and that was that he was the leader Crvena Zvezda football fans and that he been arrested in Croatia but I don't know why. I read that in newspapers but I didn't pay too much heed to all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the first part of your answer about football fans.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, was the leader of the Crvena Zvezda football fans, and I myself rooted for Partizan, and the two teams were fierce competitors.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: From their arrival in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, i.e., from your first encounter in Dalj, what was your relationship with Radovan Stojicic, Badza? What kind of contacts did you have with him?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have any special contacts with Badza, i.e., I never called him or asked him things. It was only when he arrived in the government's courtyard or in the government's building that I got to see him. And later, he attended the government sessions, but he stayed only during the first item of the agenda and he spoke about some situation on the ground. That's how the thing was presented to us. And as soon as he presented his case, he would leave the government's session. He never stayed for longer than ten minutes, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did Radovan Stojicic, Badza, attend all the meetings of the government of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem that you yourself attended?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he did not. I don't know. In percentages, he may have attended a half of them, but I'm not sure. Because he wasn't duty-bound to attend government sessions. He attended them at his own will.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When he did attend the sessions of the government, what did his participation consist of? What did he say? What was the content of his presentations to the government?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the situation on the ground. Because we wanted to know the number of dead on our side because we did not have any contacts with the villages in the area, and we didn't know what was going on. Telephone lines were down. We didn't have all-terrain vehicles to tour the villages, so we had to accept what he told us. That was our only source of that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And did he also give instructions to the government, to the members of the government, or to yourself personally at some of those sessions?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We were not in a subordination relationship. He was independent from us, we were independent from him. We had our own programme. We did what we did. And when he came, he only attended the first item. He was not interested in any of the political issues or our political decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did he ever object to a government's decision? Did he ever say that a decision should not be implemented or that it should be revised or that some higher authorities should be consulted, I mean, in Serbia or in Yugoslavia, before a decision of that kind was passed?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he never said that in so many words. Or, rather, none of our decisions concerned any of the important things. The only influence Badza exerted was when the minister of the police was being removed from office and that was not at a government session but, rather, he did it through his associates. Once he told me that Boro Bogunovic could not be the police minister because the Serbian police would not want to co-operate with him. I didn't say that -- when he said that he would be the TO commander, he also said that he would take over the police, and effectively he did that because the police were under him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that you took over the police, what police do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean the police that had been the Croatian police before the war and those officers who left the Croatian MUP and joined the police of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. Later on they were joined by some civilians, and they all got uniforms and weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You say that later they were joined by some civilians. What civilians did you have in mind? I'm reading what's in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From before the war, there were not that many active-duty policemen, so when police stations were set up in villages and somewhat larger places, the core membership were former active-duty policemen but the number had to be increased. And there were, therefore, civilians who were locals but were civilians before the war who joined those newly established police stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who was involved in the selection procedure before those civilians could join the police force?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It was not an issue to be discussed by the government. I suppose they were selected by the former pre-war active-duty policemen who chose their associates. And obviously Badza and Zavisic at higher levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to what you have told us about the demand to remove Boro Bogunovic from office as the police minister, did you receive any other indirect instructions or requests from Badza? Did he want the government to do something else or not to do something else?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't receive any instructions, either direct or indirect. Although this matter involving Boro Bogunovic might be called an indirect instruction. He didn't tell me: Remove Boro Bogunovic. He told me: Do as you will. However, if Bogunovic remains, minister, we will not co-operate with him. At least that's how I understood him. Although it's probably the same, in a way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did he tell you why? Did you ask him about the reasons why he told you that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. Of course I did. Although I already knew the reason. The problem was that he -- that Boro was not professional. He didn't have any experience. When we set up the government, he was like an interim solution to the problem that we had. That was the most important thing. He was just not professional enough. He did not have the required knowledge. I don't remember any other details.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you say that to Bogunovic? Did you convey that to him, this conversation that you had with Radovan Stojicic, Badza?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I told him. Since Boro is my friend, I tried to explain, first of all, indirectly, and then he wouldn't accept that. And then I said we could not exist and he asked: Whose position is that? And I said: That is Badza's position. And he said: Who is Badza? I don't recognise Badza. And I said: Badza represents Belgrade, and this is the position of Belgrade. I see that somehow he agreed to be deputy prime minister rather than minister of police. Although he never really worked as minister of the police. He was in Sid and he was involved in humanitarian matters to a larger degree. However, this really hit Boro bad, and I don't know why.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you said that this is the position of Belgrade, too, what were you actually trying to hint at? Did you know that this was the position of Belgrade, as you had put it, or did you say that to him for some other reason?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said that in order to cheer him up and to make him relent. He was very obstinate. He had even quarreled with Badza and I didn't even know about that. He said: No way, what do I care? And I said: How are we going to work? How is the police going to work? And then ultimately he agreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was he convinced that the request for his removal was made by Badza only or did he think that some authority superior to Badza had asked for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. That's a leading question. Counsel is just now feeding suggestions to the witness rather than the witness just giving his own account of the events. We object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't believe that it is a leading question. The witness has the option to -- to respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It's a suggestion, Mr. President. And, sure, the witness doesn't have to lead where counsel is trying to take him. But counsel is leading the witness rather than just allowing the witness to describe it. He could ask the question differently, in our view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I agree with Mr. Stringer, Mr. Zivanovic. Please rephrase or move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you say what kind of impression you had of your conversation with Bogunovic that had to do with the request to have him dismissed from the position of minister of the interior?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Bogunovic had overestimated his role. He thought that Belgrade meant somebody above Badza, although nobody in Belgrade had known of Bogunovic. And he took that very personally. He thought that this was some kind of directive from Belgrade but it wasn't. Nobody knew who Bogunovic was over there in Belgrade. Half of Slavonia didn't know who Bogunovic was anyway. Maybe it's my fault. I could have put it in harsher terms, but I didn't want to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether you could see what the relationship was like between Radovan Stojicic, Badza, on the one side, and Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, on the other?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That question was put to me when I gave a statement to the investigators in 2003, and I think about that often. I personally never saw them -- I mean, I never saw them at an official meeting either, so I couldn't see who was superior to who. But for me, they were part of the body of the same state, in a way. They were not opposed to one another.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether you met Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, and what your relationship was?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it would be hard for me to explain this concept of "relationship" here. There was no relationship. I only saw him when he wanted that to happen. I never took the initiative for these meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what happened during these meetings that he initiated? Did he make certain proposals to you, certain requests, demands, suggestions?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, basically he would say that my security was threatened, that the Croats would pay someone to kill me, that they would send a terrorist group, and I think that wasn't true and there was no reason for that. And he said that my security detail was not properly trained, that I should be taken care of by professionals, that he had people who were capable of doing that, that I would not have any costs involved for this security detail. And, of course, I thought that was unnecessary, and in a skillful way, I managed to avoid this. But, still, I was cautious. I could not say this openly, what it was that I thought. In a way, these were his main objections up until that situation concerning the plan, but that was later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When he said that your security detail should be professional, did he say to you who these professionals would be, the ones who should take over your security?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, yes, I've just said that. His people were supposed to provide for my security and then that would be proper, and I would not have any expenses involved. But, of course, I refused that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And can you tell us whether you had any security then at all; and, if so, who was it that was on your security detail?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no security before I arrived Dalj. Whenever I went to Serbia, I always had to ask someone to come with me because I had no documents. When I was in Dalj, a few days later, while I was walking through Dalj on my own because I could not just go on sitting there at the library all the time, in the street I bumped into a good friend of mine. For a while, he was my karate trainer. He was the best-known karate man in Slavonia, Baranja, at the time, Ljubo Mudrinic. He was also just walking around, he did not have any particular duties in Dalj. He was a refugee from Osijek. We chatted a bit. I asked him whether he wanted to keep me company, in a way, because he was sort of lost in Dalj too, and he agreed, and then he started just being there with me. When I got a car - it was a old Renault 25 - Ljubo and I took turns driving that car. He was not a very good driver. He said that himself, that he was not. And he suggested that he call another friend of mine who used to work in Germany who was a professional driver. He was a truck driver in Germany. So he suggested that he join us too. His name was Milenko Japundzic. He was also a professional karate man. So he showed up very quickly, the beginning of September, and he was the one who drove us. They were my security detail during 1991, the two of them only. Everybody knew that because they were popular in Slavonia and Baranja, especially Ljubo Mudrinic. That was the best-known name in sports then in Slavonia and Baranja.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you refused Arkan's offer but that you were looking for a way and, I mean, you did not want to say what the real reasons were for that. In a way, you were being cautious. Can you tell us now what the reasons were, why you did not accept his offer to have his men provide security for you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is what I was thinking about. What I heard from my driver, how he beat up that lieutenant-colonel, and I saw that he held everything under his own control. He would not allow for any improvisations. If I were to accept his security, I think that I would simply disappear. I didn't mean disappear physically but I couldn't say anything without him. I would depend on him, and I didn't want to agree to that. And I didn't go into any political topics with him and no other topics either. In his presence, I didn't even mention Partizan, the football team that I was a fan of, because I didn't know how he would react.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: After this conversation and this refusal, did you have the impression -- or, rather, how did this develop further? Was this kind of request made by him yet again for this security? I mean your security.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were a few things in the beginning, and I thought that this was a coincidence. When I showed up, he would show up. I thought that this was a coincidence, but when it happened for the third time or the fourth time, I realised that he was sort of following me. I became suspicious, and it did not feel right. I felt uncomfortable.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you say whether you thought about this, why he would be following you? What was the reason for that, these several situations when you would show up somewhere and then he would show up too?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was this problem that was following me everywhere, that I was Croatia's man, that I was in favour of negotiating with Croats, that I had been given an injection in Plitvice, that I was drugged, that I was not safe. So I thought that, in a way, he was checking on that. Because when I was in released from Plitvice -- well, it had nothing to do with Arkan. This was earlier on. A group of men showed up, and they went to local communes and they were lobbying against me. They were asking for my removal, and they were saying that I had been drugged and that I was working for the Croatian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And was there some other way, I mean, in which you were shown that he was actually following your movement?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did not have a service that could report that to me. I was on my own with these two drivers. But I had already noticed that this was no coincidence that he would show up. He came in front of the government building, he came to the government yard, he'd show up on the road. It was impossible for that to be a coincidence. It's a very small area but still. That dilemma was resolved towards the end of the year, when the Vance Plan was discussed. (redacted) [Confidentiality partially lifted by order of the Chamber]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I should now like to go back to one matter we've discussed before because I think it needs more clarification. We will go back to the arrival of Radovan Stojicic, Badza, in Dalj in the beginning of August 1991 and your first meeting with him and the group that arrived with him. Can you tell us how large was the group that came with Radovan Stojicic, Badza?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the group that I then saw in Dalj?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my rough estimate, there were perhaps ten to 12 men with Badza and about ten with Arkan. Because they were wearing different uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what kind of weapons the people in the group had? You only described the weapons of the four men who entered your office.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only those four that I mentioned had Hecklers. The rest were also armed but with automatic rifles. At least the men that I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could we clear up one more thing concerning that conversation you had about Boro Bogunovic and his dismissal from the post of minister of the interior. When did that conversation take place?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I talked to Boro Bogunovic maybe in the end of November or in the beginning of December. It's more likely December. I'm not sure. I can't remember when Boro was replaced, when he became deputy prime minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, could you tell us, to the best of your recollection, and what impressions you had about the relationship between Arkan and the JNA.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My impression was that there was no difference between the two, that they were one body.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: From what did you draw that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I was able to see not only in media reports but also on the ground, they co-operated constantly, they were constantly in touch. As much as I was able to see because I was often away.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to see that somebody from the JNA publicly criticised the conduct of Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, and the members of his unit?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of any such thing. If it happened, I never saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You were able to see during the trial a large number of reports that members of the JNA sent out, describing some acts by Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, in a very negative light. We can look at some of them again, such as P103. It's tab 78. You can see that the title of such documents was: "Information." In the left upper corner, it says that these documents were sent to the Security Administration of the Federal Secretariat for National Defence. If you wish, you can take a look. You will see that it says here that Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, conducted badly towards some officers of the JNA. More specifically, a reference is made to Lieutenant-Colonel Jovanovic. Did you ever receive a piece of information of this kind from military bodies? Did they convey such information to either you or the government? Did any military body do that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have never received any information from the army. When I say "never," we never received any information from the military whatsoever, not only the information of this kind. When I say this, I mean in an official form. Colonel Ristic did attend a government session and we spoke to him. So when I say "never," what I have in mind is official communication. There may have been some brief notes or notifications but that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did he inform you that Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, i.e., his unit, had committed crimes in the territory, that they were involved in some matters that were against the law or were not in keeping with the law?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nobody ever informed us about that, including the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you possibly receive such information indirectly through some civilian bodies of authority, either from Serbia or from Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you gain an impression about the relationship between Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan's units, on the one hand, and the units of the JNA which were deployed in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem at the time? Was there a relationship of superiority or inferiority between them?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My impression was - and it still is - that Arkan was a part of that system, that he was subordinated to them. I don't know who was whose superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say you don't know who was whose superior, do you have in mind individuals from the JNA or do you perhaps think that Arkan may have been superior to the entire JNA?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I mean individuals at lower levels. When there was an operation, I didn't know whether a major was in charge or whether Arkan had -- had the lead. I don't know -- I didn't know who was in command. Of course, I know that Arkan was not superior to the JNA as a whole, as a military.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you familiar with an initiative or a document issued by the JNA, according to which Arkan's unit or, rather, him and his unit, should withdraw from the area and go back to Serbia or, rather, Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember any such thing. I'm not familiar with that, if there was a thing like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see P3115, please. It is tab 1326. Oh, sorry. Sorry. It is P2715. Tab 742. Actually, we -- we put 1D328, but we established that this document has already been admitted into evidence. On our list, it is 1D328.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is an interview that General Panic gave in 1994. I believe that the date was 4 October 1994. I believe you remember this interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm interested in page 37 in the original, which is page 35 in the English translation. The question starts already on the previous page, on page 36, i.e., 34 of the original and the English translation respectively. The question is about Arkan and other paramilitary units as they were called at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On the page that I am showing you now, you will see where it says that they were supposed to go back, Arkan and his unit, but that Goran Hadzic, the president of Serbian Krajina, kept them as his personal security detail. Can you find it? Did you find it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But this is not correct. They were never my own personal guard. I never advocated their stay. It was not up to me to decide whether they should stay or go. I was the president of the Serbian Krajina only from 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us - and you said already that there were two people who were members of your security detail in 1991 - but later on, from the moment you became the president of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, which was in February 1992 until the end of 1993, who were the men in your security detail?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me try and remember them. Milenko proposed a relative of his who was a policeman in Baranja. His name was Perica Obradovic. Since we extended the escort, we had another vehicle so we needed another driver, so Perica proposed his own father who was a professional driver, Milan Obradovic. Then I invited my friend from Vukovar who had trained karate together with me, Savo Petrovic. Perica Obradovic then invited his best man, who had been at the police academy in Zagreb together with him, Velibor Ilincic; he was a refugee in Belgrade. And we were joined by Jovan Vranic, who was also a refugee from Zagreb, and Jovo Batalo [phoen], a refugee from Cepin who drove the third car. I believe that I've given you all the names. And then at the end of 1993 or in the second and a half of 1993, I had two locals from Pacetin who joined us. And for a short while, Ljubinko Kukic from Borovo Naselje was also together with us. That was in 1993, I believe. Velibor Ilincic had already left my escort detail by then, whereas Ljubo Mudrinic was killed in 1992, so obviously he also was no longer my security guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You told us about Ljubinko Kukic, that he was with us. Where was he from?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was from Borovo Naselje.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were all these people your security guards at the same time, or did they act as your security guards at different periods of time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During those three years, 1992, 1993, 1994, they were my security guards but not at the same time. Some joined and some left. But these are all the ones that I remember from that period when I was the president of the SAO Slavonia and Baranja. And there were only two, Ljube -- Milenko and Ljubo Mudrinic. And the others, they were with us in 1992 and 1993 but in different periods of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please repeat the names of the two guards who were with you while you were the prime minister of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a driver, Milenko Japundzic, and a security guard, Ljubo, Ljubomir Mudrinic. Both were from Osijek.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did any of the men whose name you have -- names have you just told us belong to the Serbian Volunteer Guards of Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, none of them. They were all locals. They were all Croats. From current Croatia or the former Socialist Republic of Croatia, that is. They were Serbs. They were not Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: While you were the president of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, did General Panic or anybody else from the military talk to you about Arkan and their possible wish to remove them from the Republic of Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nobody from the military ever spoke to me about Arkan. They never wanted to talk to me about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On page 36 of the original statement, which is page 34 in the translation, General Panic says that Arkan was there, as he puts it, i.e., in the territory of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, even before the military launched its operations. And he says that he had made an arrangement with local leaders. When was it that the military launched its military operations in that territory; do you know that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first operation started on the 2nd of May in Borovo Selo, and they remained there thereafter. The following one was on the 7th of July in Tenja, and they remained there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were they still there after the operation in Dalj on the 1st of August, 1991?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, since we were talking about Dalj, I thought that it went without saying that once they arrived Dalj they stayed there, so I mentioned these two things that happened before Dalj.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Arkan came there to Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem in agreement with some local leaders?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Objection to the leading question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could you rephrase, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know with whom Arkan had agreements in terms of coming to Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem and whether he had any agreements of that kind in the first place?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. When I saw him, I saw him with Badza. And I don't know who it was that he had reached agreements with before that, if any.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In this statement of General Panic's, it is stated that he ordered the local commander of the JNA to place Arkan under his control and that Arkan agreed to that. Do you have any information? Do you know of any such thing? Do you know anything that could either confirm or deny that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't have any direct knowledge what Panic ordered, but I think it was obvious on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On page 38 of the original, or, rather, 36 of the English translation, it says that at various meetings in April, May, June 1992, Arkan was mentioned. This is what I would be interested in -- actually, General Panic is speaking there. So did you attend these meetings?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not attend. I was not present.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please take a look at P152. It is tab 111.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is what I wanted to ask you. Did you know that the command of the 12th Corps was in Dalj?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew, but I did not know from the very outset that they had come, and I did not know when they came. But later on, I found out when Biorcevic was the commander, when General Bratic was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a document stating that weapons are being given to three men as war trophies. I'm interested in the person under number two, and it says here that this person is the deputy commander of the Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem TO. Can you tell me whether you knew about that; and, if so, when was it that you found out?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never knew that Trajkovic was deputy commander. And I never knew that Badza had a deputy in Slavonia and Baranja, or, rather, that he had appointed a deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And did you know that Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, bore the title of the commander of the Special Volunteer Unit of the -- of the Territorial Defence of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know about that. This is the first time I hear of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we take a look at P237.140. Tab 186.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You do remember this order. It was shown earlier on. I see that it was signed by Milanovic, Milan. You know why -- or, rather, it says here in big letters that it's Ilija Kojic, but do you know whether this is Ilija Kojic's signature?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was signed by Milan Milanovic instead of Ilija Kojic because the date is the 21st of December, 1991, when Ilija Kojic was in hospital. He was seriously wounded. He barely survived. He was still in hospital. I think he was still in hospital in Belgrade then, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, because it is written here that this order was issued by the minister of defence, was the government aware of this appointment?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And I was not aware of it either. And the government wasn't made aware of it, either officially are unofficially.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us about the relationship between Milan Milanovic, on the one hand, and Radovan Stojicic, on the other?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that they had a very good relationship, and Milanovic was Stojicic's guide through Slavonia for a certain amount of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, Mr. Hadzic, when Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, offered his men to you as a security detail, physical security, what was your impression of the sincerity behind that offer?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had the feeling that this offer was not sincere, that there was something lurking behind. I didn't know what, though. My suspicion was that what was behind it was some kind of a wish to exercise control. I had these strange things happening and first I thought that these were coincidences. I've already said I would show up in the road and he would catch up with me in the car, and I thought that was just by chance. And then afterwards, when I returned from somewhere where I was just with two other men, he said: Why did you go there? It's dangerous there. And I thought: How did he know? How did he know where I was when he wasn't even present? And I had the impression that he either had my phone bugged or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see, please, P1836.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Tab number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is tab 419.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you remember, this is a piece of information from the JNA. It's about Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan's attack against a military man on the 22nd of February, 1992, near the Vukovar Hospital. There's a description here of what had happened. But I would like to ask you to tell us about what had happened and especially to tell us how come it happened that Arkan was there at the same time when you were.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I first saw this information now, when I came here. I never knew that this was written up. I remember that I had announced my visit to the hospital and that I went in two cars. I just heard from the drivers from the second car who stayed on in the yard that Arkan had a physical fight with someone, but I did not know why or anything else. Now I see that it's this Lukic. I knew him too. He was military police, but he was a local person there in the municipality of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us the following: At the time when you went on this visit, did you know that Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, was going too? Did you agree with him that he should also come along? How did that happen? Do you know how come he showed up there?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not reach any kind agreement with him, and I do not know how it was that he showed up as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It says here that you arrived there around 2.30 on that day, accompanied by four vehicles. Did you have four vehicles escorting you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was in one vehicle, and there was one vehicle escorting me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: There's a description here of that incident now. Did you see that? Did you see what happened? Where it says here that Arkan got out of -- or, rather, got out and tried to enter by force, were you present?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not present. We passed that way and we went to the entrance on the right so this remained behind us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "we entered," who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to the vehicle that I was in. One vehicle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could we go to the next page in English, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] We can move to the next page in B/C/S, too, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And did you see or, rather, did you notice anything as you were leaving the hospital? Did you see an incident there, or did you see anyone who had been injured? Did you see anything happening?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, the door was open, and we raced through in the car. We didn't notice anything. As far as I heard from the escorts who stayed behind, it wasn't that there was anybody injured there. It was a physical fight in the sense of slapping around, but it wasn't that anybody was injured. It wasn't a big fight.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see, please, P3115.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you remember, that's an incident that occurred in 1993, in October, on the bridge at Batina, in the same place Arkan was involved in an incident with members of the Belgian battalion of UNPROFOR. Could you please tell us, to the best of your recollection, what exactly happened?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That incident was reported in the media. At that time, I already had a chef de cabinet and two secretaries, and it was the usual procedure, when going to Baranja, that one of them announce me to the police in Baranja that I was coming. And then one car of the Baranja police would meet me halfway across the bridge where the Republic of Serbia finishes and Baranja begins, and then they would turn on the rotating lights on the roof and escort me with two vehicles. And that's how I passed through. It's not the same as the incident at the hospital where Arkan's car was just behind mine. He was rushing behind us. He was in pursuit but he was not part of our motorcade. Otherwise I would have seen it. He was 5 or 6 kilometres behind us when we were on the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's clear up one thing. That first time, which is not similar to this situation, you say that he was part of your motorcade. Did you notice him in the motorcade as you were driving towards the Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't, but he turned up immediately. I understood that he had been parked outside the hospital, waiting for us. In the other incident, he started out behind us. He appeared six to ten minutes after I passed through. The time intervals are different. That's why I thought it was not the same case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This time, did you expect him to be part of your escort when you were crossing the Batina bridge?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not expecting it, and it was not part of my escort. From Erdut to Baranja, you have to cross the territory of Serbia, and there was no need for anybody to escort me. I mean, driving across Serbia, there were no war zones there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When did you learn about this incident on the Batina bridge?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That same day, while I was in Baranja for an Assembly session, I think it was. Two or three hours after the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever have occasion to talk to Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, about these incidents? Let me split this question. Concerning this incident at the Vukovar Hospital, how did he happen to be there?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we were not on such terms that I would have been able to discuss it with him. I didn't want to interfere with his movements. And I couldn't do anything about their behaviour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that this incident involving the Belgian battalion was widely publicised, did you ever ask him how it had come about that he had arrived ten minutes after you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was going on his own business, and I didn't interfere with that, but men from his detail complained about it to people from my detail. They talked about the fight, fist-fight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, I see you're -- you'll move on to another topic. But you realise that we have been discussing an incident at the Batina bridge on the basis of a document on the screen of which we have only seen the cover page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we'll see the other pages too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see the second page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this report, which describes the incident, it says it happened on 9 October at 11.14. You crossed the bridge at Batina with a police escort. Is it consistent with the truth?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It also says that at 11.25 on the same day, a convoy of three civilian vehicles arrived. The first vehicle neglected the first stop at the first check-point until members of UNPROFOR stopped them at the second check-point. Were you there?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If you look at this timeline, I was, by that time at least, 15 kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think you also have the translation of this document which has been admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have a translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I will read this out to you and I will ask you to confirm that it is the same as what you heard: [In English] "The driver of the first car just gave a sign, all soldiers left immediately the cars. They immediately armed their guns, pointed them at the soldiers on the check-point and at all important locations from where the platoon could react, in a well-prepared way. Some of them tried to replace the road obstacles and it was at this point that Master Corporal Gusbin got hurt at his head. He was hit with a rifle-butt." [Interpretation] Did you hear that one of the members of the Belgian battalion was injured?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] "When the obstacles had been removed, the first car intended to continue. The P1 commander jumped on the front of the car after having his pistol armed. "The company commander went on the spot and saw the P1 commander being beaten and hit on head and back by rifle-butts. Corporal Rutte tried to get on the M113, which was stationed on the bridge to take possession of the MG.50. As he was unarmed, the soldier hit him at the throat with the butt of his rifle. Then the P1 commander was hit again, this time at his face with the barrel of a gun." [Interpretation] Did you hear about those details?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I only heard about a fist-fight.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we scroll down a little bit, please. [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] "The company commander tried then to discuss diplomatically with the chief of the Arkan soldiers (the driver of the first car). He rejected the responsibility of the incident to our P1 commander. The company commander asked him that his soldiers don't aim anymore the UN personnel, this to decrease the tension. The Arkan soldiers did this but they succeeded to take three weapons of the UN personnel (at the end of the incident they gave back these weapons)." [Interpretation] This was paragraph 6. Do you know, did you hear that they had seized - albeit temporarily - some weapons from UNPROFOR soldiers?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, I already asked you about this but I'm going to go into more detail now. The men who came with Badza and Badza himself, did they ask you where they could find accommodation? And you said no. I'll show you a document that has been reviewed at length during the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's P194.140.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Tab number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tab number 152.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Have you seen this order? I should like to ask you: Have you ever signed this order?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never. And I never heard it -- saw it before The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The signature that you see on this document, is it yours?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: How do you explain your signature on this document, if you say you had never seen it before coming to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't sign it, but it doesn't mean that the signature is not mine or very similar to mine. I could have given an autograph to somebody and then somebody could have copied it or placed it on a different paper. I don't know anything about forgery because I've never forged anything myself, but I've never signed an order like this, and I didn't know that the order existed. And I never heard of these concepts that are mentioned here. Starting from the top, for instance, the Secretariat of the President, did not exist at all. All of it is completely false. It's entirely a forgery. Then the next thing, I, as prime minister of the Autonomous District, I had no right to make such a decision without the government. And also this concept: Conclusions of staff commanders. I've never heard of such a thing. During the entire war, I never heard of conclusions of staff commanders. Even if we put this document aside, no such thing existed. Staff commanders did not exist as an institute. At least I never heard of it. And if we look at the date, 21st September, Arkan was already at the centre at that time. He had already occupied it. Why would he need this paper? All that I've said, I said as a layperson. I'm not an expert in these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe there is a mistake in the translation of the first sentence which reads: "Pursuant to the headquarters commanders' conclusion ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll come back to this part a bit later. But something else I wanted to ask you. The date here is the 21st of September, 1991. Could you please tell me whether Arkan and his unit had been in the centre already before that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, they were in the centre perhaps seven, eight, or even ten days before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When Radovan Stojicic, Badza, arrived with him and when he introduced him to you, can you tell us, if you remember, what exactly did he tell you about Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan? How did he present him to you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that he told me this, if I may quote him: He will be the commander of special units. But I didn't know whose units those were. I didn't understand whether that will be the TO or the police or his own units. I didn't understand that. The only thing I understood was that there was some special units from Serbia. But that's the extent of my understanding at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me one more thing: At the time when this order was allegedly drafted, according to the date on it, had the government already been set up? Was there a government of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not officially. There was an Assembly on the 25th [as interpreted] September and that's when the government was established. I'm not sure that on -- on this particular day we already had stamps, but it is possible that we did, on the 21st of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think it is appropriate time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, we noticed one error in the transcript. It is on page 2, line 6, and line 14. Namely, as a result of this error, the Defence document 1D762 was admitted as D124. Actually, 1D275 had to be admitted as D124.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, according to the Registrar's note, 1D762 was shown on the screen and admitted. Are you trying to convey that 1D725 was on the screen and admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. The document 1D275 had to be admitted as D124.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We're just trying to get on the same path. 1D275 has indeed been shown but then 1D72 -- 1D ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: 1D7 -- then 1D762 was shown. Now, when you tendered -- you asked to -- that the document should be admitted, did you mean 1D275 and we admitted 1D762. Is that what happened?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That's what happened. Okay. If we substitute the admitted document, the result will be that 1D762 is not tendered and not admitted. Is that what should happen?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I recall, 1D762 was shown to the witness, but, right now, I cannot recall what -- what is this document -- what was this document. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: -- I double-check if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: -- we ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- for the moment --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: -- for this document to be tendered. Yes, we -- we'd like to have 2 -- 1D275 as D124.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Madam Registrar, can we substitute the document and have 1D275 admitted and marked as 1D -- as D124. So the answer is yes. And then you take your time, Mr. Zivanovic, to check what, if -- if anything needs to be done with 1D762.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll double-check it and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: -- get back to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Before I continue -- oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a proposal.
