Sometimes the Defence counsel or the Prosecutor present a document, first one and then the next one, and then they tender that document, and then the Registrar says the document is admitted but we don't know which one. It is much better to first state the number of the document under which it is presently listed and then under the number which it is admitted. Would that be a suitable proposal?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could be a good suggestion, Mr. Zivanovic, that you and -- and OTP, if that's the case, would repeat the document number that you asked to be admitted. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before I continue, I -- I would indicate to one translation error in the document. It is in first paragraph. We submit that the part -- the part of sentence of the first sentence was not correctly translated. It reads: "Pursuant to the headquarters commanders' conclusion ..." Namely, the translation booth correctly translate this part of sentence at page 45, line 8. It reads: "Pursuant to the conclusions of commandants of the staffs."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We agree with that, Mr. President. We looked at it over the break and actually we've asked that the document be sent to CLSS just to do a translation so that it's correct. And when it is received, we'll move to substitute it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Noted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, you said that there was no office of the president or a Secretariat. Do you know if there was a Secretariat of the Government; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was the secretary of the government. I don't remember whether he had an office or not. I know that there was just one staff member and that was him, and I don't know whether there was anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us his name.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His name was Jovica Pejakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see P1809.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Tab number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Sorry. It is tab 406. Sorry. It is tab 406. Thank you. However -- however, we asked the -- the translation is not the same as the original of document, because we asked translation of assignment of Mr. Jovan Pejakovic. It seem there is no such translation of this document. Okay. We'll remove ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The Registrar tells me that there is only one page in English and two in -- in B/C/S. Would that explain the problem? Or is the translation another document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It seems that the decision on assignment of Mr. Pejakovic was not translated, so I'll skip this document. Or I -- I could read just one sentence. It is just one sentence of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, would you have an objection to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, this is a decision on appointment. Under 1 it says: Jovan I. Pejakovic, a lawyer by profession, is hereby appointed as the secretary of the government of the Serbian Autonomous District of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. I'll skip Article 2 because it is not important. And the date is 10 September 1991. My question is this: Do you remember this appointment?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, just to make sure, is what -- the document you were just reading to Mr. Hadzic, is that the document we have on the screen in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You spent a long time working with Mr. Pejakovic. You knew him well. Would you say that Mr. Pejakovic would write in the heading "the Secretariat of the Government" as we saw in the previous document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we return the previous document? Can we bring it back on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I was about to object to what sounded like a leading question in terms of how Mr. Pejakovic prepared the documentation that he wrote. And I think it was suggesting to the witness that the documentation was prepared in a certain way rather than simply asking how Mr. Pejakovic prepared it. Maybe I'm being oversensitive but I think that there was a suggestion. And also I don't know that the witness has yet testified that he knew Mr. Pejakovic well and worked with him a lot, or words to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could you --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The previous -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The previous document just suggests what Mr. Pejakovic was and that he was well aware of his position. And I do not really understand it as a leading question, but I could rephrase it as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I don't -- I don't think - and I think Mr. Stringer pointed that out as well - that it is really a leading question, but the foundation -- the foundation for the question would -- would be appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Apologise for the interruption, sincerely. Just to inform the Chamber that the same decision on appointing Mr. Pejakovic is in evidence at L57, which is the gazette in its entirety, and so at page 14 of the English translation, the Chamber would be able to actually see the decision in L57.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We don't think that we need to have that on the screen, Mr. Stringer, but thank you for the suggestion. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see the previous document, 194.140, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Hadzic, in your presence, did Mr. Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, ever introduce himself as the commander of the special units of the Territorial Defence of the AO Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never. He never introduced himself that way in my presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any explanation concerning this document?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My explanation -- well, I'm going to say something now. I'm not sure whether it's relevant or not, but I think that Arkan didn't need this document. It was made later. Perhaps for the purposes of some defence here before this Tribunal. But that is just my assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us something about whether the government of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem financed this centre of the Territorial Defence or, rather, this unit that Zeljko Raznjatovic had? Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The government of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem did not finance that centre or that unit. Also, in my presence, the government never discussed any of that. I never heard anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see, please, P215.140.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, sorry. It is tab 170.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: With the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tab -- sorry. Tab 170.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You remember this document that was shown. Can you tell us -- actually, can you tell us whether you know anything about this problem that is referred to in this document?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I first saw this document here. I never knew anything about this. When I say "here," I mean the Prosecution. I don't know whether it was Investigator Vladimir Zuro [phoen] that showed it to me, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know that at some point in time, the expenses of the government and of this centre were dealt with cumulatively, as is stated in this document?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And did Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, perhaps familiarize you with that problem, that they tried to get him to pay for the expenses of the government as well?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether the government of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem or later on, in general, Republika Srpska, or, rather, the Republic of Serbian Krajina - sorry - whether -- whether they covered any of the expenses of this unit?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, no, never. I could hear about this in the media because Arkan bragged in public that he covered his own expenses, and I heard that several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In which respect did he claim that? How did you understand that? Did he provide an explanation? How was it that he himself covered the expenses of this unit that had, say, 100 members, according to some of the information here?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can say how he explained it, and, of course, I can give you my understanding of that, if that is relevant. He said that he is not anyone's burden in any way, that he finances his own unit through sponsors from Serbia. That was my understanding of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And did he ever ask for any kind of financial assistance or any assistance from the government or from you personally?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, attend meetings of the government of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not attend regularly. Sometimes he would come in, spend a few minutes there, and then leave. According to what I remember, it was very rarely. It's not written here, but I said that when Badzo [as interpreted] was present at a session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did he take part in the work of the government in any way through some proposals of his, suggestions, requests?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not take part. And before the government sessions, he never discussed the agenda with me. He was simply not interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did he ever say that the government should not make any decisions before consulting him or Badza or some third person from Belgrade, something like that? Do you remember whether any such thing ever happened?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember any such thing, and I don't think that anything like that ever happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Two times you mentioned some conversation you had with him during the time of the Vance Plan, so now I'd like to ask you to tell us what that was all about, what kind of conversation this was.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will try to explain briefly. It is well known that Milan Babic and the western Krajina rejected the Vance Plan and that Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem accepted the plan. At the time, when this was in the making and when the Vance Plan was being negotiated and when it was already known that Babic would reject the plan, we in the eastern part had already agreed, my ministers and I, that we would accept that. However, we had not stated that publicly yet. Once Arkan came to see me unannounced and he started talking about that plan, which took me by surprise because he never talked about political developments. As a matter of fact, I thought that he did not even know what was going on in the political sphere at all. Whenever he was in contact with me, he always behaved as a big Serb, a big Serbian patriot. He never glorified Slobodan Milosevic. I thought that he was some kind of opposition to Milosevic. I even thought that there could be a problem with him if we were to accept that plan, that he could create certain problems. However, all of a sudden, he started threatening Babic in front of me, although Babic was not there. Babic was in Knin. And I remember what he said exactly. I can even quote that. He said: What does Milan Babic think? Does he know who it is that he is opposing and who it is that he does not want to obey? He is not obeying our president, Milosevic. That's the first time I heard that from his mouth, that he thought that Milosevic was his president. He also said something else that surprised me even more. I saw something then that I hadn't seen before that and that I never saw after that in the case of any human being. You could no longer see the pupils of his eyes, the way he rolled them. You could just see the white, and he said: Does Babic know that we are going to kill him and all the children he has and all the relatives he has if he does not accept that? Then, in a way, everything was much clearer to me. He didn't address threats to me but to Babic, and then I understood there won't be any problem because our government decided to accept the peace plan because Arkan considered that should be accepted and that nobody would have to kill my children.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, was he already familiar with the position of your government, although you hadn't publicly expressed it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said at the beginning, if you followed me, that the position was not yet known to Arkan or to official Belgrade. It was a decision of a narrow circle of ministers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please clarify what you've just said, that nobody would kill your children. What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I knew that my government would accept the plan. We have already accepted it at that moment and there won't be any problem. Because I understood the message: Whoever fails to accept the plan, his children would be killed. That, in fact, was a message directed at me, not Babic, as I finally understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: During that conversation, did you understand the threat was serious, that he actually means it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood it was very serious, 100 per cent serious. And I thought at that moment that Arkan must have been sent by someone to tell me that, but to this day, I don't know who it could be.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if he had a similar conversation with anyone else from your government, for instance, or from your circle?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. Because I was very often away from Erdut, and it's possible that he also talked to some ministers about the same conclusion, that the plan needs to be accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see P144, please. It is tab 105.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you remember this interview? You had occasion to read it here during the Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember seeing it here, but I don't remember the interview itself or the context in which I gave it originally.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was it an authorised version of your interview? In other words, were you given this text to review before publishing?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't. I just talked to the journalist, and I'm not sure that he even recorded it. He only made notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Look at the third subheading in the English translation. You were discussing the general situation in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, and you said -- it straddles page two in English. You describe the situation, but what I want to ask is this: At that time, on 4 September, did you know what the general situation in that area was, and if you did know, what were your sources of information?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was born in that area, and I knew the situation from before the war. I knew which villages were Croat or Serb or mixed. And the other information I obtained from media reports, to the extent I was able to follow them, because I didn't have a special information service that would keep me posted on the situation on the ground. I also heard some things from ministers who toured refugee centres, and I met with refugees on the other side of the Danube myself. And I had a lot of information which was sometimes accurate, sometimes exaggerated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said, among other things, that the situation was the best in Baranja, that 80 per cent of that territory had been liberated. Did you visit Baranja at some point during the month of August 1991?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure it was in August but perhaps early in September, I went to Baranja once, when it was possible, before the Croatian authority was established there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said, among other things, that the state of affairs was the worst in Western Srem. Did you have occasion to travel there?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. Because, as I heard towards the end of June or the beginning of July, at the time of the attack at Tenja, there was also an attack at Mirkovci village, and from that time until complete liberation, Mirkovci had been completely encircled for nine months. That entire area, Mirkovci, Sidski Banovci, et cetera, they were isolated. They couldn't go to our places, we couldn't go there. They had a border -- a boundary with Vinkovci. They couldn't go there. And on the Serbian side, there was the village of Slakovci that was inaccessible to them, so they just couldn't -- had nowhere to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You say, among other things in this interview, and I will quote this passage: "Croat old-timers, known as Sokci, are passive. Croats, Herzegovina men, Dalmatians, even Zagorje men, all of those who settled there after 1941, they are very dangerous as they know that one of our goals when we gain control is to return all Pavelic's volunteers, to turn them back." Can you tell us did you really put that way; and if you didn't, what is this supposed to mean? What did you exactly say?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is certain that I didn't put it the way it is written here. I was explaining to the journalist that there had been no problems between Serb old-timers and Croat old-timers who had lived in those areas for hundreds of years, just as my family had. You have to know that Slavonia and Baranja is a plain. These people are tamer and quieter, more peaceful. The problems were caused by Croats and Serbs from mountainous regions, such as Dalmatia, parts of Bosnia, et cetera, and maybe he left out that part because he had some vested interest of his own, and he left only this reference to Croats. But it is certain that in my experience at least those people from mountainous regions tended to be more radical in their behaviour in 1991. More aggressive, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Below, talking about the JNA and the Serbian fighters, you say, among other things: "All of us, the government and primarily the people, are in favour of resolving this peacefully and democratically regardless of the fact that we have tragic experience with Ustashas from 1941. We don't believe that the Croatian people are Ustashas. We believe that there are good forces there who will understand our problems, who will understand that we cannot live together anymore, that neither of them -- neither them nor we want to live together anymore, that that must be resolved at last. We must draw the line." Tell me, was it the stance of your government and your personal stance? And what did you imply?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The stance of the Serbian Democratic Party from before the war was common knowledge. We discussed it yesterday and the day before yesterday. My stance was that we need to negotiate with the Croatian side, and that was the reason why they attacked me or called me drugged or a traitor. That was the basic point. All the other conclusions follow from that. I'm not sure I put it exactly that way, but I did think that if Croatian people were allowed to determine their own fate and what they were going to do and how they're going to live, Serbs should be allowed to do the same. People should not get killed over it. I'm not quite sure that this interpretation is 100 per cent accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the box, under the subheading: "The quota of slaughter" --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's on the following page in English. Sorry, page 1. It's the middle passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You talk about information about the massacre of Serbs in Vukovar. Can you tell us how you obtained that information? Did you go to Vukovar at that time? I mean, before, before this interview.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not. As I've already told you, I heard that from refugees or they learned that from their families and relatives. But these are the conclusions reached by the journalist. This is not my way of expression. I never used the word, I did not with an extra "I." It's his comment and his words.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is the next page of translation, sorry. Third page, sorry. Third page of the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's a title here: With Serbia in Yugoslavia. The journalist asked you, amongst other things, or, rather, he said that people hold it against you that you live in Novi Sad and not in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. You provided an answer. Could you tell us whether this answer reflects what you told the journalist?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does. My children were refugees. I didn't mention Kragujevac, however, my children went there for sleep-overs with friends. They didn't spend any time there as refugees. The best illustration of the way I was informed and how well I was informed at the time was the fact that I didn't even have a telephone line at the time. I expected that it would be connected the following day but it didn't happen. I believe that this clearly illustrates the seriousness of my position. I didn't have a telephone line; hence, I couldn't get by any information.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to your seriousness as a person or the seriousness of the institution that you represented?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not my personal seriousness but the seriousness of the government or the government in the making that I represented and the position that I held at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: There's also a reference to the problem which you had with the idealogy and the symbols of that idealogy. Could you tell us whether your words are truthfully conveyed here; and if they are not, would you please tell us what you actually said at the time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when I reflect on that now, I know this newspaper. I believe that this is a Montenegrin newspaper, the official newspaper of the Montenegrin government or the ruling party. I believe that the journalist was mindful not to say anything that didn't suit the government in Montenegro. At that time we did have some problems with idealogy, especially at the beginning of that summer, the months of June and July. I had problems with Radojica Nenezic, as I've already told you. A lot more positive is said here about Communism than I would every say or think. I don't know whether the journalist misunderstood me or whether he decided to misinterpret me ever so slightly. Because I believe that the five-pointed star was an ideological symbol; whereas it says here just the opposite, that I didn't consider it an ideological symbol. Obviously we were talking at cross-purposes, the journalist and I.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And finally in this text you also spoke about the western borders --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is next page of translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Inter alia, you said: "The Ustashas have realised that we can no longer live together, but they believe that they can deal with that by either killing us or chasing us away." Was that a general belief, i.e., that the extremists among the Croatian forces really wanted to move the Serbs out of the area or kill them if they didn't want to move out, whether that was the official Croatian policy?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With hindsight obviously we know much more. You have a complete picture of what happened in 1995. I can only tell you what I thought in 1991. We knew that during the Second World War the official policy of the Ustasha government was to chase away one-third of the Serbs, kill another third, and the last third of the Serbs were to be converted to the Catholicism. Obviously now all the cards are on the table, and the third option was out of the window, so only the two options were still viable and that was either for us to be killed or chased away. And we said that we wouldn't accept any of the two and that we would fight for our rights. And now whether I was right or wrong was later proved by what happened during Operation Storm in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, I wanted to move to another topic and that is the beginning of the month of September, when you had talks with some representatives of the international community who arrived in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. Can you tell us just briefly whether you remember any of those talks. Who did you talk to? Why? What was the reason why you met them?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that I met with Mr. Henry Wijnaendts and Geert Ahrens. They arrived from Belgrade, they had crossed the Danube river. I can't remember all of the topics, however, the main issue was to negotiate to cease-fire and to sign a cease-fire with the Croatian side. Before that, several cease-fires had been signed but they all fell through. Somebody suggested - I don't know who - that I should put my name on a document of that kind on behalf of the Serbian side, to reinforce that document. I thought that a cease-fire was absolutely necessary, that's why I supported that idea. I didn't see any harm in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any problems during your talks with Messrs. Wijnaendts and Ahrens?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no problems during the talks. The problem arose when the document was put on the table before it was signed. I was supposed to sign it on behalf of the Serbian people and Vladimir Seks signed on behalf of the Croatian parliament, I believe, or perhaps the Croatian government. I believe it was the Croatian government, not the parliament. I apologise. I didn't want to sign because there was no equality of arms. He was not signing on behalf of the Croatian people but on behalf of the government; whereas I was supposed to sign on behalf of the entire Serbian people, not only the government. So I refused to sign. I gave them my condition but the negotiators did not accept my condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that Mr. Seks signed on behalf of the Croatian government, was he there? How did he sign?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His signature was already on that piece of paper. He himself was not there, not in person, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And on that day but a bit later, did you, after all, sign this agreement?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at the end of the day, I did sign it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Why did you change your mind? How come you signed the agreement after all? First of all, what was the essence of that agreement? Was the document acceptable or unacceptable for you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The agreement was good for us. The gist of it was to cease-fire and that was the most important thing, to stop people dying. In my view, this was just a technical matter. However, I could not sign on my own behalf. I had associates with whom I had to consult. I didn't do anything on my own, neither as the president of the SDS, let alone as the prime minister of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. This was a utopian position, a majority of the minister thought if that I signed as the representatives of the government, the international community would recognise us. I thought that it was nothing but pure utopia. They insisted I sign but I couldn't because I didn't have the mandate to sign any such document. And then somebody in that delegation - I believe that it was either Mr. Wijnaendts or somebody who had come with him - made a break and consulted somebody in Belgrade. I was called to come to the phone in the elementary school in Borovo Selo. That's where the troops were. That was the first time I went in. I often passed by but I never went into the school. I went upstairs to the first floor. There was a communications centre there. They gave me a -- a telephone, a metal telephone, like a field telephone, and they told me: Slobodan Milosevic wants to talk to you. And I thought that they were pulling my leg. I answered. I recognised his voice from television. He spoke to me very kindly as if we had known each other for a long time. He asked me what the problem was. I told him. And then he said: Why is that a problem? It's better for you to be the representative of the people. That's much broader than being just representative of the government. He tried to persuade me, but that was not necessary because I was already convinced that that agreement should be signed because it was a cease-fire agreement and that couldn't be bad. And then he said: Come on, sign this. Let's start living in peace. We've had enough of war. So I said: Okay, I will. And then I returned to a group of my associates who were there. I communicated that position to them, especially to those who were against me signing that document at first. I told them that I'd spoken with Slobodan Milosevic and that it is in the interests of Belgrade, Serbia, and the SFRY as well as our -- ours to sign that document. Then they changed the mandate that they had given me in order to allow me to sign that document, which is what I eventually did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think it is appropriate time for break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic. Thank you very much. We'll adjourn till tomorrow morning, 9.00. Mr. Hadzic, I remind you that you're still under oath. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 10th day of July, 2014, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.59 p.m.,
